reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD & ACG
clinicalPearls: Caused by obstruction of hepatic venous outflow anywhere from the small hepatic veins to the junction of the inferior vena cava and right atrium, producing hepatic congestion
The classic triad is abdominal pain, ascites, and hepatomegaly, though presentation ranges from asymptomatic to fulminant liver failure
An underlying prothrombotic state is present in most patients, most notably myeloproliferative neoplasms (including JAK2-associated disease), so a thrombophilia workup is essential
Doppler ultrasound is the usual first-line test, with CT or MR venography to define the level and extent of the obstruction
The caudate lobe often drains directly into the inferior vena cava and is characteristically spared and hypertrophied while the rest of the liver is congested

Management is stepwise: anticoagulation for essentially all patients, then angioplasty or stenting of short-segment stenoses, transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting, and finally liver transplantation for refractory or fulminant cases
Acute presentation with rapid-onset jaundice, coagulopathy, and encephalopathy represents acute liver failure and is a medical emergency
Chronic outflow obstruction leads to congestive fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis with portal hypertension
reference.pathophysiology: Obstruction of hepatic venous outflow raises sinusoidal pressure and causes hepatic congestion, hypoxic injury to hepatocytes, and centrilobular necrosis. The resulting portal hypertension produces ascites and, over time, congestive fibrosis progressing to cirrhosis. Most cases stem from thrombosis on a background prothrombotic disorder, commonly a myeloproliferative neoplasm, inherited thrombophilia, antiphospholipid syndrome, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, pregnancy, or oral contraceptive use; in some regions membranous webs of the inferior vena cava predominate. The caudate lobe, with its independent venous drainage into the vena cava, escapes congestion and hypertrophies. Speed and completeness of obstruction determine whether the course is fulminant, acute, or chronic.
additionalDifferentials: Right heart failure or constrictive pericarditis causing hepatic congestion
Cirrhosis from other causes with portal hypertension
Malignant infiltration of the liver or vena cava
additionalInvestigations: Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic veins and inferior vena cava as the initial test
CT or MR venography to map the site and length of obstruction and assess caudate lobe changes
Thrombophilia and myeloproliferative neoplasm workup, including JAK2 mutation testing
Liver function tests, coagulation profile, and assessment for encephalopathy to gauge severity
Ascitic fluid analysis and, where needed, liver biopsy or hepatic venography
redFlags: Acute liver failure with jaundice, coagulopathy, and encephalopathy requiring emergency specialist and transplant assessment
Rapidly worsening liver function or tense refractory ascites
Concurrent inferior vena cava obstruction with lower-limb oedema and renal impairment
Evidence of an aggressive underlying myeloproliferative disorder
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the rapidity and extent of obstruction and the response to a staged treatment strategy. Many patients do well with anticoagulation and interventional or shunt procedures, but fulminant presentations carry high mortality without transplantation, and untreated chronic disease progresses to cirrhosis.
pitfalls: Attributing ascites and hepatomegaly to more common cirrhosis and missing outflow obstruction
Failing to search for and treat an underlying prothrombotic disorder, allowing rethrombosis
Delaying escalation from anticoagulation to interventional or transplant options in deteriorating patients
Misinterpreting caudate lobe hypertrophy as a mass lesion
management: Start anticoagulation in essentially all patients, using heparin followed by an oral anticoagulant, to prevent thrombus propagation

Identify and treat the underlying prothrombotic disorder, including cytoreductive or JAK2-directed therapy for a myeloproliferative neoplasm and specific treatment of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria or antiphospholipid syndrome
Relieve short-segment hepatic vein or inferior vena cava stenoses and webs with angioplasty and stenting as the next step in refractory outflow obstruction
Place a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt when angioplasty and medical therapy fail to control congestion and portal hypertension
Manage portal-hypertensive complications with sodium restriction and diuretics for ascites, variceal surveillance and treatment, and treatment of encephalopathy
Refer for liver transplantation in fulminant hepatic failure or disease refractory to interventional therapy
Monitor liver function, vessel patency on imaging and, in established cirrhosis, undertake hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance
Coordinate care between hepatology, a transplant centre and haematology

Escalate: emergency hepatology and transplant assessment
Doppler ultrasound of hepatic veins and IVC; liver function and coagulation profile
CT or MR venography to define the level and extent of obstruction
Start anticoagulation; thrombophilia and JAK2 workup
Short-segment stenosis or web amenable to angioplasty?
